newsitem.title: PERU: Japan backs Peru's unflinching stand with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Japan backs Peru's unflinching stand with rebels.

text.p: Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto vowed not to give in to "terrorism" on Monday, reinforcing Peru's unflinching stand against Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

"Japan will never give in to terrorism," Hashimoto told parliament in Tokyo at the first session of the new year. "Terrorist activity is a grave challenge to all states and societies and it is vital for the international community to tackle terrorism in unity."

Hashimoto reiterated his "complete confidence" in Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's hardline negotiating tactics in refusing to consider the rebels' main demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades.
The Peruvian government and rebels gave no ground on Monday to allow a start to the peace talks they have been edging toward for more than week.

Both sides say they are ready to negotiate, but a meeting remains on hold because the goverment rules out considering rebel releases, which the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) insists be discussed.
With both sides stuck in their uncompromising positions, Japanese task force in Lima stepped up efforts to ease the ordeal for the hostages kept under the gun for the 34th day.

The Japanese arranged to play soothing tunes to the hostages via a local radio station. The songs, two Japanese and one Spanish, were to have a relaxing effect and cheer the captives, a task force spokesman said.
The station would also play "radio gymnastics" -- tunes to which listeners carry out stretching exercises popular in Japan -- he added.
The captives heard Mass on Sunday from the Vatican's representative due to sit on a negotiating commission, Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori.

The VIP hostages also received counselling from a captive Jesuit priest who has rejected a chance at freedom to help those left behind -- including government and security force officials, two ambassadors and dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

The rebels have started to use their captives as workhands. One of the hostages spent nearly an hour at the front of the compound on Sunday taking batteries from cars parked outside the building into the home.

The hostage, identified by witnesses as Japanese Embassy official Akihisa Ouyigama, lifted the hoods of two vehicles and removed the batteries -- apparently required by the rebels as material for radios.
The day before, Ouyigama and another Japanese diplomat appeared on the roof of the besieged residence to rearrange rebel banners whose message was concealed after they twisted in the wind.

The difference between the Peruvian government and the MRTA over the release of jailed rebels has been the same since Dec. 17, when the 15 heavily armed guerrillas stormed a reception at the diplomatic mansion taking more than 500 hostages.
The MRTA released most captives in the first weeks of the standoff but since New Year's Day, only one hostage has walked free for medical reasons.

The two sides have agreed that Cipriani, a Red Cross representative and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, a former hostage in the siege, will sit on a "guarantor" commission to oversee talks, if and when they take place.
Fujimori, whose younger brother, Pedro, is among the captives, received another boost for his tough line in handling the crisis.

A poll of 400 people in the capital released on Sunday showed that Fujimori's popularity had grown during the siege. According to local pollsters Analistas y Consultores, approval of Fujimori's government rose to 50 percent in January from 43 percent in December.
While Fujimori has refused to bow to the rebels' demands, he was willing to consider allowing them to leave the country if they free all the hostages and lay down their arms.
